parsed_answer.content:
Java bytecode portability has historically carried a performance tradeoff compared to ahead-of-time compiled languages like C++. To bridge this gap, modern Java Virtual Machines incorporate a sophisticated Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation subsystem. Instead of interpreting bytecode instruction-by-instruction indefinitely via the template interpreter, the JVM dynamically monitors execution profiles, identifying code blocks that consume disproportionate CPU cycles, known as hot methods. Once a method crosses specific invocation and backedge (loop) thresholds, the runtime transitions it into natively optimized machine code.

Tiered compilation bridges the gap between startup latency and peak throughput by employing multiple compilation tiers. Typically, the JVM starts in interpreter mode (Tier 0), quickly collecting profiling data. As methods warm up, they transition to C1 (Client Compiler or SimpleJIT, Tier 3), which inserts profiling instrumentation while generating fast native code. Finally, heavily executed hot methods graduate to C2 (Server Compiler, Tier 4) or Graal, where aggressive, profile-guided optimizations—such as escape analysis, method inlining, and loop unrolling—are applied. Deoptimization occurs when these speculative optimizations are invalidated by runtime behavior, forcing the execution frame to safely drop back down to the interpreter or a lower tier.

rows: Fast native code without instrumentation overhead
Peak execution throughput via aggressive optimization

items: Hot methods are identified using invocation counters (tracking how many times a method is called) and backedge counters (tracking loop branch executions), which trigger OSR (On-Stack Replacement) if a long-running loop needs to be compiled mid-execution.

Tier 3 utilizes Method Data Objects (MDOs) to record precise type feedback, branch Taken/Not-Taken probabilities, and virtual call site receiver frequencies, feeding critical data directly into C2 optimization phases.

Deoptimization invalidates compiled code dependencies when class hierarchies change or speculative type assumptions fail, reconstructing exact interpreter frames from optimized machine state using OSR buffer maps.

parsed_answer.content: Frequent deoptimization (often visible via -XX:+PrintCompilation logs showing 'trap' or 'unusual trap') is a massive performance killer. It typically happens when polymorphism ruins monomorphic call sites, or when null checks are unexpectedly violated. Ensure your design avoids unnecessary type mutations in hot execution paths to keep code stably compiled at Tier 4.
